DHS inspector general is now evaluating the rise in detainee deaths and has opened a probe into the use of force in ICE detention, which increasingly includes Tasers, pepper spray, and restraint chairs.

Less than two weeks after he died, ICE reported another death at the same facility. A June GAO report found that man was placed in a medical holding room, not a suicide-resistant cell, and left unattended despite showing risk factors for suicide.
Lunas Campos is one of 20 people to die in ICE custody so far this year, a toll that is on pace to set a record for annual deaths in immigration detention.

His family lawsuit alleges four guards restrained him on the ground and kept pressure on his neck and chest, even after he yelled that he could not breathe, until his body went limp. DHS says he was trying to take his own life and died in the ensuing struggle.
In November he went four days without his medications. On Jan. 3, a cellmate says staff repeatedly refused his requests for medication before he was moved to segregated housing.
Three months before he died, guards found him with a sheet tied around his neck. Staff discussed moving him to a higher level of mental health care, according to the records. They never did.

Lunas Campos had bipolar disorder and anxiety. Medical records reviewed by The Washington Post show he repeatedly told staff at Camp East Montana in El Paso that he was not getting the care he needed for his mental illness.

The El Paso County medical examiner ruled the death of Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old man in ICE custody, a homicide by asphyxiation. He died in a struggle with guards at a privately run detention center. 🧵

What’s the Alternative? Instead of Detentio

Earlier this year I drove out to the Hagerstown site. The 825,000 sq ft building is in Williamsport, a town of 2,000 people. At planned capacity, 1,500 detainees would nearly double the population. The building has four toilets and two water fountains.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/…

Four warehouses are still being converted to ICE detention centers. The four sites are in San Antonio and Socorro, TX; Surprise, AZ; and Hagerstown, MD. The report argues these communities should not feel economically cornered and should demand alternatives.

A detention center creates what the report calls an "economic dead zone." Retail shops, restaurants, and offices are less likely to locate near a jail than near a vacant warehouse. Libraries, health centers, and commercial spaces attract further development and employment.

Documented alternatives also include health clinics, indoor farms, commercial office parks, and community churches. In the San Fernando Valley, a 1940s supermarket warehouse became a medical campus featured in The Architect's Newspaper.

A former Walmart in McAllen, TX was converted into a public library. A former big-box store in Moorhead, MN now houses food science kitchens, welding labs, and large lab spaces for a high school career academy. A warehouse in Greenville, England became a skate park.

The report describes warehouses as having high ceilings, no internal columns, heavy load-bearing floors, and large-scale operational capacity. Those qualities make them structurally adaptable for almost any use except, the authors note, housing people behind bars.

ICE's "Detention Reengineering Initiative" set a goal of jailing 92,600 people on any given day and deporting 1 million people per year. Buying and converting warehouses was the mechanism for reaching that scale.
